meta.title: Who really said "God gets you to the plate, but once you're there you're on your own"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Halberstam's Summer of '49 (1989) has Williams saying "God gets you to the plate." His own autobiography ends it differently — and this familiar ending is untraced.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'God gets you to the plate, but once you're there you're on your own'?
meta.ogDescription: A named book does carry the first half of this Ted Williams line — but not the ending everyone quotes. Here is what the record actually shows.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder, the last man to hit .400
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Williams’s and it is in print — but not in these words. David Halberstam’s Summer of ’49 (William Morrow, 1989) reports it as a habit of speech, “God gets you to the plate,” Williams would say, with no date, occasion or transcript attached; Williams’s own My Turn at Bat is quoted for a different ending, “but it’s up to you what happens when you get there.” The familiar close — “once you’re there you’re on your own” — has never been traced to a page. Baseball Almanac ↗, which names a book or magazine for most of its Williams quotations, files this one as “Widely Attributed.”

source.excerpt: God gets you to the plate, but once you’re there you’re on your own.
trail: A full-text search of scanned books ↗ returns twenty-six titles carrying the phrase. The earliest located is David Halberstam’s Summer of ’49 (1989), where it is something Williams “would say” — a Pulitzer-winning reporter’s secondary attestation, decades before the quote-database layer existed. The rest, from Pat Riley’s The Winner Within (1993) to later motivational anthologies, come after it and cite nothing.

Baseball Almanac’s Ted Williams page ↗ lists twenty quotations by him. Seventeen name a book, magazine or encyclopedia — sixteen of those with a date; three — including this one — are filed as “Widely Attributed,” the tag used when no publication can be named.

Wikiquote’s Ted Williams article ↗ sources its quotations to My Turn at Bat, the Boston Globe, the New York Times, Ken Burns’s Baseball and other named works. This line does not appear on it in any section. Simple English Wikiquote ↗ does list it — under “Sourced quotes,” referenced back to Baseball Almanac’s “Widely Attributed” tag, which is the circular citation in miniature.
A Quote Investigator site search ↗ for “gets you to the plate” returns no articles, so the specialist literature on quotation origins has never taken this one up.

The open-web layer beyond the books is quotation databases — AllAuthor ↗ and its peers — each carrying the line with an author name and no citation, and most carrying the same two transcription errors.
source.excerptNote: Three endings circulate for one thought. Williams’s autobiography is quoted for “but it’s up to you what happens when you get there”; Halberstam prints the opening clause alone, glossing it as Williams meaning that his eyesight and physical gifts got him to the box and what he did there was his own; and the databases supply “once you’re there you’re on your own,” most often garbled to “but once your there your on your own” — the version the aggregators print ↗. It is the ending, not the thought, that has no home.
source.rightsNote: No publication can be tied to this exact wording, so its copyright status cannot be settled on its own terms — and every attested relative of it is in copyright: Williams’s My Turn at Bat (1969) and Halberstam’s Summer of ’49 (1989) alike. Anything Williams said dates from his playing or post-playing life, well after 1931, so no route to the public domain exists here in any case. Quotle.info makes no public-domain claim for this wording.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.kicker: The man it is credited to
author.heading: Who was Ted Williams?
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder, Hall of Famer, Marine Corps aviator
author.bio: Theodore Samuel Williams — Teddy Ballgame, The Splendid Splinter — played his entire major-league career for the Boston Red Sox, 1939–1942 and 1946–1960, and finished with a .344 average, 521 home runs and the best on-base percentage in the game’s history. In 1941 he batted .406, and no big-leaguer has reached .400 since. He was absent from the Red Sox roster for 1943, 1944 and 1945 as a naval aviator, was recalled in May 1952 to fly F9F Panther jets in Korea, and entered the Hall of Fame on the first ballot in 1966.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest located print appearance: Halberstam, David. Summer of ’49. New York: William Morrow, 1989 — reporting “God gets you to the plate” as something Williams would say. A near-identical sentence is attributed to Williams’s autobiography — Williams, Ted, and John Underwood. My Turn at Bat. 1969, p. 3 — in the wording “I have a God given talent. God gets you to the plate, but it’s up to you what happens when you get there” (page number per Wikipedia’s reference; not yet checked against the book). The circulating ending “once you’re there you’re on your own” is attested in neither; Baseball Almanac, “Ted Williams Quotes,” lists that form with its source given as “Widely Attributed.”

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: There is no rival author here, and no fabrication either. The problem is narrower: the thought is Williams’s and it is in print, but the ending every quotation site prints is not the one his own book gives, and those sites have all been copying one another.

items.who: BrainyQuote, QuoteFancy, TheySaidSo, AllAuthor and the rest of the quote-database layer
items.why: They publish it under his name with no book, date, interview or broadcast attached. AllAuthor’s entry ↗ is typical — a quote, an author line, and nothing else.

The dominant circulating form reads “but once your there your on your own” — two homophone errors reproduced identically across sites, including AllAuthor ↗. Text transcribed from a printed page does not usually arrive pre-broken in exactly the same two places everywhere.

items.who: The reference works that do cite their sources
items.why: The English Wikiquote Ted Williams page ↗ sources its entries to My Turn at Bat, the Boston Globe, Ken Burns’s Baseball and similar — and does not include this line at all. Neither Halberstam nor Williams’s autobiography gives this ending; the books attest the thought, not the sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Williams said something very close to this, and two books say so — Halberstam heard it as a habit of speech in 1989, and his own My Turn at Bat is quoted ending it “it’s up to you what happens when you get there.” What nobody has produced, as of August 2026, is a page for this ending; the baseball reference that lists it is candid that it cannot ↗. Until someone does, “once you’re there you’re on your own” is a paraphrase in circulation, not a quotation with a source.

context.heading: Why this one is hard to pin down
lead: Williams is among the most quoted hitters who ever lived, and a great deal of what he is quoted saying reduces to the same idea: nobody can do this part for you. He wrote The Science of Hitting ↗, he spent decades telling younger players that the work at the plate was theirs alone, and the collection of his sayings is thick with variations on that theme. A line about God getting you as far as the batter’s box and no further fits that voice — and here, unusually, the books bear the fit out.

What they do not bear out is the wording. Halberstam gives the opening clause; the autobiography gives a different close; the databases give a third. The test that matters is dull — which page, which broadcast, which day — and for “once you’re there you’re on your own” nobody has answered it: not Quote Investigator ↗, not the English Wikiquote article, and not the baseball reference that lists it under his name and then declines to say where it came from.
context.detailsSummary: A tell in the wording itself
detailsBody: The version that actually dominates the web is not the tidy one. Aggregators overwhelmingly print it as “God gets you to the plate, but once your there your on your own” — two homophone slips, reproduced identically from site to site. Text copied from a printed book tends to arrive clean and then drift; text that arrives already broken and stays broken in exactly the same places was copied from another database, not from a page. It is not proof of fabrication, but it does mean the chain of custody runs back to a website, not to a source.

The religious framing, by contrast, is not alien to him at all. Several biographers called Williams an atheist, but his autobiography ↗ is quoted against them — “I’m not a religious man, but I do believe in God. I believe that he has given me a gift, and I try to use it as best I can” — and the same book supplies precisely this framing about his own talent. The SABR biography ↗ is silent on his beliefs, discussing only his mother’s lifelong Salvation Army work, but silence in one source is not absence from the record. The God language supports the attribution; only the ending is in doubt.
context.pull: The thought is his. The ending everyone quotes belongs to the databases.

sourcesVerified.claim: Baseball Almanac lists "God gets you to the plate, but once you're there you're on your own." among Ted Williams's quotations and gives its source as "Widely Attributed"; of the twenty quotations by him on the page, seventeen name a book, magazine or encyclopedia (sixteen of those also carry a date — the exception is "Sport Magazine's All Time All-Stars", given with no date or publisher) and three are marked "Widely Attributed".

Wikiquote's Ted Williams page sources its quotations to works including My Turn at Bat, the Boston Globe, the New York Times and Ken Burns's Baseball, and contains no quote mentioning "God gets you to the plate"; it has no Misattributed or Disputed section.
A Quote Investigator site search for the phrase "gets you to the plate" returns no results ("Nothing Found").
AllAuthor prints the quote as "God gets you to the plate, but once your there your on your own." credited to Ted Williams, with no original source or publication cited.

SABR's BioProject biography gives Ted Williams's birth as August 30, 1918 in San Diego and death as July 5, 2002 in Inverness, Florida; career 1939-1960 with the Boston Red Sox; .406 in 1941; Hall of Fame 1966; 39 combat missions in Korea in 1952-53; his mother May Venzor Williams devoted her life to Salvation Army work; the biography contains no discussion of his own religious beliefs.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame records Ted Williams as inducted in 1966, Boston Red Sox 1939-1942 and 1946-1960, career .344 average, 521 home runs, .482 on-base percentage (best all-time), .406 in 1941, born 1918 in San Diego and died 2002 in Inverness, Florida.

Wikipedia gives Theodore Samuel Williams, August 30, 1918 - July 5, 2002, Boston Red Sox 1939-1942 and 1946-1960, career .344, .406 in 1941, Hall of Fame 1966 on the first ballot, naval aviator in WWII and F9F Panther pilot recalled May 1, 1952 for Korea, nicknames including "Teddy Ballgame" and "The Splendid Splinter", and his books My Turn at Bat (1969) and The Science of Hitting (1970).

The English Wikipedia Ted Williams article states: "Williams was called an atheist by several biographers, though Williams disproved this in his autobiography by stating that he did believe in God" (cited to Williams & Underwood, p. 7); "As quoted in his autobiography My Turn at Bat, Williams stated: 'I have a God given talent. God gets you to the plate, but it's up to you what happens when you get there'" (cited to Williams & Underwood, p. 3); and "I'm not a religious man, but I do believe in God. I believe that he has given me a gift, and I try to use it as best I can" (cited to Williams & Underwood, p. 137). The page numbers are Wikipedia's references and have not been checked against the book itself.

An Open Library full-text search of scanned books for "God gets you to the plate" returns 26 results. The earliest work is David Halberstam's Summer of '49 (first published 1989, W. Morrow), whose snippet reads: "...them that was important. 'God gets you to the plate,' Williams would say, referring to the fact that...". Later hits include Pat Riley's The Winner Within, Triumph and Tragedy in Mudville, Extraordinary Comebacks and 1001 Motivational Messages and Quotations for Athletes and Coaches.

Simple English Wikiquote's Ted Williams page lists "God gets you to the plate, but once you're there your on your own." under the heading "Sourced quotes", referenced only to Baseball Almanac's "Ted Williams Quotes" page (retrieved 2009-09-20) — the same page that files the line as "Widely Attributed".
